title: What to Do With a $500K Inheritance
summary: Before investing an inheritance, it's important to know how taxes come into play. Learn how to manage a $500,000 inheritance and associated taxes.
body_markdown:
You inherit $500,000 and your first instinct is to figure out how to invest it. But before choosing stocks, mutual funds or other investments, there are important decisions that can have an even bigger impact on your financial future. Your first move is important. One mistake and you could hand over thousands of dollars to the IRS.


## Know What You Have and What You Can Do With It


You can’t make smart investment decisions until you know which assets you’re dealing with. Different assets follow different tax rules, and those rules can affect whether you should hold, sell or reinvest.


Cash, for example, has no immediate federal income tax when you inherit it. That gives you the flexibility to invest it whenever you’re ready.


Taxable brokerage accounts, on the other hand, often receive a[stepped-up cost basis](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/stepped-up-basis) , which resets to the investment’s market value on the date of death for tax purposes. So, if you sell inherited investments soon after receiving them, you may owe little or no capital gains tax.


Not all inherited assets get this treatment, though. Inherited[traditional IRAs](https://smartasset.com/retirement/traditional-ira) are treated differently. Withdrawals are generally taxed as ordinary income, and most non-spouse beneficiaries must empty the account within 10 years of the original owner’s death.


Real estate, however, is closer to the brokerage account example. Real estate can receive the same stepped-up cost basis as taxable brokerage accounts. If you sell the property, that adjustment may significantly reduce or eliminate your capital gains tax.

## This Mistake Can Cost You Thousands


How you take money out of an inherited IRA can set your investment plan back by years. For example, let’s assume you inherit $500,000: $200,000 in a taxable brokerage account holding stock that your parent bought for $100,000, and $300,000 in an inherited traditional IRA.


The brokerage account receives a stepped-up cost basis, resetting your cost basis to $200,000. If you sell the investments immediately after inheriting them, you generally would not owe[capital gains tax](https://smartasset.com/taxes/state-capital-gains-tax) on the $100,000 of appreciation during your parent’s lifetime.


The inherited IRA is different. If you withdraw the full $300,000 in one year and already have $100,000 of taxable income, your total taxable income goes up to $400,000.


For tax year 2026, the additional IRA income would be taxed as follows:1


- 22% on $5,700 = $1,254
- 24% on $96,075 = $23,058
- 32% on $54,450 = $17,424
- 35% on $143,775 = $50,321


Your estimated additional federal tax would be $92,057 before deductions, credits and state taxes. This figure reflects the extra tax caused by the withdrawal itself, not your total tax bill for the year, which would be higher once tax on your other income is included.


The IRS generally gives many non-spouse beneficiaries up to 10 years to empty an inherited IRA, rather than requiring a lump-sum withdrawal. Depending on when the original account owner died and whether they had begun taking RMDs, the beneficiary may also need to take annual distributions during that 10-year period.


Spreading withdrawals over multiple years may help reduce the chance that a large one-time distribution pushes more income into higher tax brackets, though the best approach depends on the beneficiary’s tax situation.

## How to Put $500,000 to Work for You


Once you’ve identified the inherited assets and their tax treatment, consider setting aside enough cash to cover each year’s tax bill from the IRA distributions, plus any other near-term needs, before investing the rest.


Then, consider investing what remains based on your time horizon. Retiring within five years and relying on this money for living expenses often calls for a conservative mix. But a 20-year horizon or longer may support a stock-heavy portfolio with a goal of long-term growth.
